title: Design Front Middle Back Queue
statement:
Build a class `FrontMiddleBackQueue`: a sequence of integers that can grow and shrink at its first position, its last position, and its middle.

- `FrontMiddleBackQueue()` starts with no items.
- `pushFront(val)` puts `val` before every item; `pushBack(val)` puts it after every item.
- `pushMiddle(val)` inserts `val` so that, if the queue held `m` items before the call, `val` ends up at 0-based index `floor(m / 2)`.
- `popFront()`, `popBack()` and `popMiddle()` remove the first, the last, or the middle item and return its value; `popMiddle()` removes the item at 0-based index `floor((m - 1) / 2)` of a queue of `m` items. Each of them returns `-1` and changes nothing when the queue has no items.

In other words, when an even-length queue has two middle spots, both middle operations use the spot nearer the front: inserting `6` in the middle of `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` gives `[1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5]`, and removing the middle of `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` returns `3`.
constraints: At most 1000 calls in total are made to pushFront, pushMiddle, pushBack, popFront, popMiddle and popBack
notes:
## Intuition

One array with `splice` at the middle works, but each middle operation shifts about half the items. Instead split the queue into halves `front` and `back`. If `front` always holds as many items as `back` or one more, the frontmost middle item is the last item of `front` and a middle insert happens at the seam, so every operation touches only the ends of the halves.

## Approach

1. Keep `front` and `back` with the rule `front.length - back.length` is 0 or 1. `balance` restores it after any change by moving one item across the seam.
2. `pushFront` adds to the start of `front`; `pushBack` adds to the end of `back`; each then calls `balance`.
3. `pushMiddle`: if `front` is the longer half, first move its last item to the start of `back`; then append `val` to `front`. The rule still holds, so no `balance` is needed.
4. Because `front` is never shorter than `back`, the queue is empty exactly when `front` is empty; every pop returns `-1` then.
5. `popFront` takes the start of `front`; `popMiddle` takes the end of `front`; `popBack` takes the end of `back` (or of `front` when `back` is empty, which means one item is left). Each then calls `balance`.

## Example 1, step by step

After `pushFront(1)` and `pushBack(2)`, `front = [1]`, `back = [2]`. `pushMiddle(3)` appends to `front`: `[1, 3] | [2]`. `pushMiddle(4)` first moves `3` across, then appends: `[1, 4] | [3, 2]`. `popFront` returns `1` and `balance` pulls `3` back: `[4, 3] | [2]`. `popMiddle` returns `3`, then `4`, and `balance` moves `2` into `front`. `popBack` finds `back` empty and returns `2` from `front`; the last `popFront` returns `-1`.

## Complexity

- Time: each method does a constant number of end operations on the two halves, so O(1) with a real deque (such as Java's `ArrayDeque`). JavaScript's `shift`/`unshift` may move elements, which is fine for 1000 calls.
- Space: O(n) for the n stored items.

## Pitfalls

- With an even count there are two middles; both middle operations use the one nearer the front.
- `popBack` on a one-item queue must look in `front`, since that is where the single item lives.
- Forgetting `balance` after a pop lets the halves drift, and the middle is no longer the end of `front`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `front` | first half of the queue; holds the middle item at its end |
| `back` | second half of the queue |
| `balance` | helper that moves one item across the seam to restore the size rule |
| `val` | the value pushed or popped |
